vignette:
The Weight of What He Carried Home

Minh is a 46-year-old Vietnamese American software engineer who came to the United States as a teenager, eventually building what most people would call a quiet, successful life — a steady career, a home in the suburbs, a wife named Lan who teaches elementary school. From the outside, the architecture of his life looks solid. Inside, it has been fracturing for years.

Before he became the man who writes code in a glass-walled office and coaches his son's weekend soccer team, Minh served in the Vietnamese military as a young man in his early twenties. He was deployed to a contested border region during a period of active conflict, and it was there, over the course of fourteen months, that he witnessed things he has never fully been able to name — not to Lan, not to his closest friends, and only recently, haltingly, to a therapist. He watched men in his unit die. He held a friend whose wounds were unsurvivable. He was present during an assault on a village that still visits him in sleep, uninvited and unchanged, as vivid as the day it happened.

He came home, and then he came to America, and he told himself that the ocean between him and those years was enough. For a long time, he almost believed it.

The cracks began to show in his late thirties, though Minh suspects they were always there, just papered over by the relentless momentum of building a new life. He started waking at 3 or 4 in the morning, heart hammering, the smell of smoke and earth so real he would get up and check the house. He began avoiding the Vietnamese New Year celebrations that Lan's family hosted — the firecrackers, the noise, the crowd — telling everyone he was tired, that work was demanding. He was not lying exactly, but he was not telling the truth either.

At work, Minh is known as meticulous, reliable, someone who can hold an entire system architecture in his head. But in the past two years, his concentration has begun to desert him. He sits in front of his monitor and finds that he has read the same function three times without absorbing it. During a team meeting last spring, a colleague slammed a door and Minh was on his feet before he understood why, his chair scraping back, his hands braced on the table. The silence that followed lasted only a few seconds, but it lives in him still.

He describes a persistent sense that the world is not safe — that something is always about to go wrong — and a numbness that settles over him in the evenings when Lan tries to talk about ordinary things: the neighbors, a film she wants to see, their daughter's college applications. He hears her voice and feels himself retreating behind glass, watching his own life from a careful distance. He tells himself he is protecting her from something she cannot understand. He is not sure anymore whether that is true or whether he is simply unable to find his way back.

The nightmares cycle through the same material: the border, the smoke, the face of his friend. Some mornings he wakes so exhausted by what sleep has put him through that he sits in his car in the driveway for twenty minutes before he can make himself go inside. He has started drinking two or three glasses of whiskey most evenings — not to feel good, he says, but to feel less. To turn the volume down on something that never fully goes quiet.

What strikes him most, he says, is the loneliness of it. He is surrounded by people who love him. He goes to work, he coaches soccer, he eats dinner with his family. And he is, in some fundamental way, still standing in that village, still twenty-three years old, still unable to leave.
